intro_en: The Israel National Trail crosses the "Land of the Craters" and encounters the unique geological phenomena and landscapes that this region offers. From the crest of the Hatzera ridge, the ridge in which the Small Crater (Makhtesh Katan) was formed, we descend to Nahal Hatira. From there we reach the foot of the parallel ridge, the Hatira ridge, in which the Yeruham Crater, the Large Crater (Makhtesh Gadol), was formed. We climb the wall of flatirons (matzle'ot) of the Large Crater on its eastern flank, and look into the crater from its rim. We descend from the crater rim to the overnight campsite at the gate of the Oron phosphate plant.
character_en: Along the segment there are 4 ascents that demand effort. Those coming from the north descend Ma'ale Yamin, climb Ma'ale Palmach with the help of a ladder and handholds, climb "the Great Fin" on a fairly prolonged ascent, and descend the flatirons of the Large Crater to Oron.
shortcuts_en: It is possible to finish at the parking area at Metzad Yorke'am, beside Road 206.
pois_en: Metzad Tzafir. Ma'ale Yamin. Nahal Hatira. Ma'ale Palmach. Ein Yorke'am. The flatirons of the Large Crater, "the Great Fin" and all the landscapes of the Large Crater.
important_en: This is a difficult route for hikers who struggle with a fear of heights. Ma'ale Palmach can be challenging, and there is no way to bypass it other than giving up Ma'ale Yamin and Nahal Hatira.
When flash-flood warnings are issued for the streams of the south and east, hiking in Nahal Hatira is forbidden and dangerous.
Between the top of Ma'ale Ali and the overnight campsite in Nahal Akrabim, drinking water can be filled at a nearby army base.
Water can be filled at the gate of the Oron plant, which is the reason the trail descends to Oron rather than continuing directly to Har Karbolet.

It is not possible to reach the Nahal Akrabim campsite by vehicle; the road is physically blocked. On the other hand, although at the start of Road 227, coming from the Dimona-Oron road, there is signage prohibiting driving on the road, this route up to the Nahal Akrabim campsite is not physically blocked. The Society for the Protection of Nature in Israel is working with the authorities to have the signage removed.
description_en:
We start walking from the overnight campsite heading west, on a dirt road, until we meet Road 277. To the right, the road comes from the direction of Dimona and Yeruham. To the left, it descends Ma'ale Akrabim (Scorpions' Ascent) towards the Zin Valley and the Arava. This is the road that linked Eilat with the rest of the country during the British Mandate and in the early years of the State.
After crossing the road we continue with the red marking along a ridge. On the left, the tributaries of Nahal Gov drain into Nahal Zin, and on the right, the tributaries of Nahal Yamin. The red marking accompanies us as far as Metzad Tzafir, an ancient fort that served as a stopping and guard point on the road that climbed from the Zin Valley via the "Roman Ma'ale Akrabim" into the Negev.
At the trail junction south of the fort, the Israel National Trail continues west (right) with the blue trail to the top of Ma'ale Yamin. To the south, the blue trail descends to the "Roman Ma'ale Akrabim". We walk a stretch through a landscape of gentle hills and gullies, until cliffs rise before us, marking our arrival at the top of Ma'ale Yamin.
A junction is marked on a rock slab: the meeting of the blue trail we have followed so far with the green trail that descends left into Nahal Yamin. Before we set out on the descent of Ma'ale Yamin, note the deep cracks in the rock slab we are standing on. In just another brief moment, lasting thousands or millions of years... the great block of rock will collapse, and boulders will tumble with a great roar into the channel beneath us.
We descend Ma'ale Yamin to the channel of Nahal Yamin. On the right we can see the great waterfall of Nahal Yamin. At the bottom of the ascent, in the stream bed, the first acacia trees appear.
After a short walk in the canyon-like channel of Nahal Yamin, we reach the confluence with Nahal Hatira. On a prominent rock we see a trail-junction marking, where the green marking we have been following meets a red trail that heads off to the left, down Nahal Hatira to the Zin Valley.
The Israel National Trail turns right with the green trail, up Nahal Hatira towards the Large Crater, from which the stream issues. Nahal Hatira collects the runoff from every corner of the crater in a wide fan, bursts out through the "Crater Gate", passes Ein Yorke'am, cuts eastward into the "Hatzera anticline", crosses it and empties into Nahal Zin in the Zin Valley.
Immediately after the right turn, a beautiful acacia tree grows at the foot of the channel's side wall. The tree and the wall form a gateway through which the trail passes, a shaded spot that invites those who wish to take a rest break.
The trail continues up the channel, which widens and then narrows again. Two young acacia trees side by side mark the bottom of Ma'ale Palmach.
In the 1940s, Palmach scouts, who were among the pioneering hikers of the Negev, climbed this ascent. They were looking for a way around the blockage formed by the great waterfall of Nahal Hatira.
The Palmach members gave the ascent the name "Naqb al-Yahud" (the Jews' Pass), a name imitating the Arabic names of the ascents in the Judean Desert that they had heard from the Bedouin. Later its name was changed to "Ma'ale Palmach".
To improve hikers' safety, a ladder and handholds have been installed where needed. After the ladder the trail passes above a high cliff. The trail is good and comfortable, but it is recommended that those who suffer from a significant fear of heights get help from other hikers and not look down...
On completing the climb up the ascent, we come close once more to the channel of Nahal Hatira, on the way to Ein Yorke'am. Before that we pass a trail junction, where a short black trail leaves the green trail to the left and leads to the waterfall and a rock pool (gev). Those who wish can walk to the waterfall and return the same way to the green trail.
After another short walk we reach the descent to Ein Yorke'am. A short red-marked trail also descends left towards the channel. On the descent there are steps hewn into the rock, evidence of the importance of Ein Yorke'am as a water source in ancient times, which led to effort being invested in making it accessible.
Ein Yorke'am is part seasonal spring, part "tamila", that is, a rock pool within a short rock gorge. Thanks to the shade cast by the stone walls, it holds water from winter into summer, depending on the amount of flooding.
A short walk from here leads to the vehicle parking area beside Road 206, where it is possible to end the hike.
After crossing the road, the Israel National Trail continues west with a black-marked trail. The trail passes beneath the railway line through a culvert, and immediately on exiting it the climb begins, in a gully that cuts between the rock "flatirons" (matzle'ot), tilted rock layers in the shape of triangles that build the eastern flank of the Hatira anticline, which here is in fact the outer wall of the Large Crater.
After a short climb up the gully with several rock steps, the trail exits to the right and climbs onto the tops of the tilted layers. The trail walks along a kind of "knife edge" up to a high point at the top of the ridge, on a section hikers call "the Great Fin".
At this point the crater comes into view: to the left and right, the walls of the crater on its eastern side, and ahead of us, across the crater, the walls of the crater on its western side. On the right we can also make out the Crater Gate, the point where Nahal Hatira bursts out of the crater. Behind us we see the channel of Nahal Hatira on the section we walked today, after it leaves the crater, as it crosses the Hatzera ridge eastward to Nahal Zin.
We advance along the trail to the crater rim, from which we can clearly see the expanses of the crater, with the walls enclosing it all around and the system of channels that drains and collects the runoff from its entire area.
At this point, the black trail descends into the crater, while the Israel National Trail turns south and walks a stretch along the crater wall. Beside the trail we can notice concentrations of fossils; these are a protected natural asset and it is important to leave them in place. At several points where the trail passes right on the edge of the steep wall, we can enjoy fine views over the crater.
The trail turns into a gully, and then the descent begins through the flatirons of the crater back to the outside of the crater. At the end of the descent we reach a culvert beneath the railway line. The trail turns right and advances a short distance at the foot of the railway embankment, up to the crossing point over the track. Please note: the track must be crossed with care, freight trains pass here!
After the crossing, the trail turns slightly right and continues diagonally to Road 206. After a few minutes of walking beside the road, the Israel National Trail turns right, moves away from the road and climbs the crater wall again. Even so, we continue walking along the edge of the road to the gate of the Oron phosphate plant, which is the end point of the segment and has an organised overnight campsite for hikers.
author_en: Itzik Ben Dov, Trail Marking Coordinator, Society for the Protection of Nature in Israel.
